name: Wendy Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We do not represent employers, AI firms, unions or government, and this interview is confidential. Tell me about an ordinary day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and manage the online product-description team for a large hardware retailer. Four editors report to me. We check sizes and safety notes, write clear listings and fix mistakes when a customer buys the wrong part. I moved from store service into this junior manager post five months ago, and even with my bachelor’s degree I am still learning how to run a publishing calendar. I use AI every day for first drafts and comparison lists, but the editors check the actual box.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the situation at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband drives a school minibus, and our children are ten and fourteen. We have a mortgage and about four months of expenses saved; my pay is ordinary for this manager role. There are some other online retail offices nearby, but school pickup and my husband’s early route make a late shift difficult. I am willing to try new tools, but I want to know who pays when a listing is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my editors AI Plateau is basically another small update to the tools we use. It can tidy a description, but someone still has to measure the bolt in the box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job stays, though the household budget is not generous. My husband’s minibus route is steady during school term, and our four-month reserve gives us room. A quiet holiday period still lowers his pay, so I would keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I’d continue the two-editor check on safety notes and use our current AI tool for first drafts only. If a new routine feature arrives, I’d compare its descriptions against twenty returned products before using it online. We would keep our monthly reserve transfer while both paychecks arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own work. The holiday weeks still need a budget, but I do not see a big new threat in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the bolt example mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a listing called a bolt eight millimetres when the package held a six. A customer drove back to the store for a refund. We fixed the bolt listing after looking at the box, not after rereading the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens during school holidays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband gets fewer minibus hours. We set aside part of term-time pay for those weeks, and the reserve covers surprises. I would not call a quiet week a crisis, but I do not ignore it.

say: **AI Plateau** tidies descriptions without changing who checks the goods.
An editor still needs to **measure the part** in the box.
think: My **online manager job** looks stable in this mild world.
School holidays lower my husband’s **minibus pay** despite our reserve.
do: **Compare** a new feature with twenty returned products before posting listings.
**Continue** transferring part of each paycheck into savings.
feel: I feel **calm** about my work, with school holidays budgeted.
S0.quote: We fixed the bolt listing after looking at the box, not after rereading the screen.
fieldNote: Her **four-month reserve** and planned holiday budget support calm in a mild AI world.
Daily AI use remains tied to **physical product checks** when a listing causes a return.

steps.text: Keep two editors checking product safety notes in 2026
Test the new feature against twenty returned products
Continue monthly transfers from paychecks into household savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will write many listings, check details and answer simple buyer questions. That may help customers find parts, but workers should be paid to check errors and learn the new publishing system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my desk is writing schedules, checking text and resolving customer complaints. I am fast with new tools, yet I am a new manager and still learning, so fewer editors could also mean no need for my post. Four months saved helps, but a pay cut would strain the mortgage when minibus hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d run a trial on returned items, recording wrong sizes and refunds rather than only how fast descriptions appear. I’d take the company’s paid publishing-system course if my director approves my place, and I’d bring error numbers to the staff council. If our team shrinks after rollout, I’d apply for posted store-training roles only if their pay and hours fit the mortgage and school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. I like a useful tool, but I cannot assume being the person who likes it will preserve my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why store training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know what customers ask when the wrong part comes home. I could show store staff how to read and fix a listing, but I have never managed a training programme. I would ask to see a day of that work before claiming I can do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the staff council ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A published error rate, paid checking time and a route for editors whose jobs change. I am not asking the company to keep bad processes forever. I want the company to count the returns a rushed listing creates.

say: **AI listings** need paid human checks and published error rates.
Editors should have a clear **paid route** into changed work.
think: A smaller team could remove my **junior manager post**.
A pay cut would strain the **mortgage** during low minibus hours.
do: **Trial** AI listings on returned goods and count wrong sizes and refunds.
**Take** paid publishing training if my director approves a place.
**Apply** for store-training roles only if pay and school hours fit.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible cut despite liking the tools.
S1.quote: I want the company to count the returns a rushed listing creates.
fieldNote: She embraces **daily AI use**, yet knows software fluency does not guarantee a manager post.
Her **store-training idea** is a possible route she has not yet practised, with pay and pickup limits.

steps.text: Trial AI listings on returned goods and record refunds
Take paid publishing training if the director approves her place
Bring listing error numbers to the staff council
Apply for store-training vacancies only if pay and pickup hours fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the editors AGI by 2028 could write and check almost any product listing cheaper than our team. We need an honest timetable and a way for customers to challenge a wrong safety note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full thinking AI in 2028 could do our writing, checking and planning. Robots that can handle stock in stores arrive around 2031, but our online desk could be cut before that. I expect most editor posts to go, and as a new lead I think my own job is likely to go too. Four months saved and my husband’s term-time pay would not cover a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I’d ask the director for notice and severance figures, and I’d meet the staff council to ask who approves safety claims after automation. In 2027 I’d apply for two posted product-safety coordinator jobs if their salary and school hours work for us; those jobs also use screens, so I would not call them safe from AGI. If AGI arrives in 2028 and I am cut, we would use our reserve for mortgage bills while I take an actual offer, not pay for a speculative course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I can make a plan, but a four-month reserve goes quickly when two children and a mortgage depend on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about safety claims?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who can stop a listing for a child’s power tool if the AI misses a warning. A customer should not discover a missing safety warning at home. I want a named person and a way to correct it immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel the planned family holiday and keep the money for the mortgage. I would tell the children before they heard it from a neighbour. My husband would keep his route; I would not ask him to take unsafe extra hours to replace my pay.

say: **AGI by 2028** needs cut dates and a human safety-claim decision.
Customers need a way to **challenge wrong warnings**.
think: Our online desk faces AGI in **2028**, before store robots around 2031.
I expect **my own new post** to go; four months saved may run out.
do: **Ask** for notice and severance figures next week.
**Apply** for posted safety roles only if pay and school hours fit.
**Cancel** the planned family holiday to protect mortgage cash.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely job loss and a short household reserve.
S2.quote: A customer should not discover a missing safety warning at home.
fieldNote: She expects **her own post** to go and does not treat another screen-based safety job as protected.
The **holiday cancellation** follows a concrete plan to preserve mortgage cash, while school hours constrain applications.

steps.text: Meet staff council about human approval of automated safety claims
Apply for product-safety posts if salary and school hours fit
Cancel the planned family holiday and keep cash for mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to test where a real person catches product mistakes. I want editors and store staff in those tests, not only the people who bought the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My writing and checking work could still be taken in 2031, with hands-on store robots following around 2034. Product-safety coordination also uses thinking work, so I would not assume it lasts unchanged. Five years gives me time to learn how safety decisions are made, but a paid vacancy is not promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From January 2027 I’d spend one paid day each month with the product-safety manager if my director approves cover for the editors. I’d take a company-funded safety course only if it happens in paid hours. Once AGI arrives around 2031, I’d apply for a safety role only if it still has authority to stop a listing and pays enough for our mortgage and school care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but I can test the work before betting the family budget. The longer warning helps only if the company gives us a real place to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the safety manager show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How a warning is checked against the actual packaging and how a listing is taken down quickly. I can write a clear sentence, but I do not yet know the whole safety sign-off chain. I would keep a list of my gaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working and use free reading at home when I can, but I would not claim that makes me qualified. My husband’s early route leaves me with most afternoon pickup. I need work time for a proper course.

say: **Five years** lets editors test product-safety work with store staff.
The trial needs a **paid place** and real stop authority.
think: Writing and product-safety desk tasks both face **2031 AGI**, even if hands-on store work changes later.
A future **safety vacancy** and company-funded course remain uncertain, so I cannot budget for either.
do: **Shadow** product safety monthly from January 2027 if editor cover is approved.
**Take** a safety course only with company funding and paid hours.
**Apply** after 2031 only if the role can stop listings, pays mortgage and childcare, and fits school pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time to test work before risking the mortgage.
S3.quote: I can write a clear sentence, but I do not yet know the whole safety sign-off chain.
fieldNote: She names a **sign-off gap** rather than assuming daily AI use makes her qualified for safety decisions.
Paid learning and **afternoon pickup** set limits on any transition.

steps.text: Shadow product safety monthly if director approves paid editor cover
Take safety course only with company funding during paid hours
Apply only if safety role can stop listings, pays mortgage and childcare, and fits school pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives a decade to build real product-safety roles and teach people while they still have wages. I would ask the staff council to review the training and pay terms each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then our children will be older, and if both wages hold we could pay down the mortgage and build more than four months saved. My current listing work faces thinking AI in 2036, and safety paperwork may too. Hands-on store robots follow around 2039, so that later date does not protect my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep checking listings against real boxes and put an extra amount into savings in full-pay months after the mortgage and school costs clear. I’d take a paid rotation with product safety if offered without a pay cut. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for a site-facing safety job only if it still pays our bills and includes real product checks, not just another screen queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy. Ten years gives me room to build the skill, but I cannot count a future safety job as income today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would extra savings look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps twenty each full-pay month after school costs, if the minibus route has all its hours. I would transfer it after the mortgage payment clears. We would skip a month rather than borrow to pretend we saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does site-facing mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walking the shelf with store staff and checking the printed warning on the actual box. Even that work may change when robots arrive around 2039. I want the job description and pay before I leave a wage I know.

say: A **decade** should build paid product-safety paths and yearly staff review.
A real safety role includes **checking boxes**, not only screen queues.
think: Both wages could reduce the **mortgage** and grow savings if they hold.
Listing and safety desk work face **2036 AGI**, before store robots around 2039.
do: **Keep** checking online listings against real boxes in 2026.
**Save** twenty only in full-pay months with all minibus hours, after mortgage and school costs.
**Take** a paid safety rotation if offered without a pay cut.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because the future safety job is uncertain.
S4.quote: We would skip a month rather than borrow to pretend we saved.
fieldNote: She makes **new savings** conditional on full minibus hours, mortgage and school costs.
Her **site-facing fallback** includes physical checks but still has AGI-exposed paperwork and later robot risk.

steps.text: Keep checking online listings against actual product boxes
Save twenty only with full minibus hours after mortgage and school costs clear
Take paid product-safety rotation if offered without a pay cut
Apply after 2036 for site safety work only with real product checks and bill-covering pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our online team could disappear before I am ready for product safety work. Notice dates, paid safety training and a real vacancy with a living wage would help. Four months of savings is breathing room, not a new career.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the store worker who opens the box whether the warning is right. The screen can say “safe” while the printed package says something else. A child should not discover a missing safety warning at home.

headlineQuote: Four months of savings is breathing room, not a new career.
portrait: **Wendy, 43**, is a newly promoted online product-description manager at a large hardware retailer with a bachelor’s degree.
Her **typical pay**, four-month reserve, mortgage, two children and school-holiday income swings shape every job choice.
She uses **AI daily** but checks real packaging and is still learning the publishing and safety sign-off chain.
She is **calm** under AI Plateau, alarmed by likely 2028 job loss and cautious about paid safety work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her new online post before she qualifies for product safety work.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **notice dates**, paid safety training and a real vacancy with adequate pay would help.
